text:
Which Pallava king, avenging his father's earlier defeat by invading and capturing Vatapi from the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II, assumed the title 'Vatapikonda' and developed Mahabalipuram as a port city?
a) Aparajita Pallava
b) Nandivarman II Pallavamalla
c) Narasimhavarman I (Mahamalla)
d) Mahendravarman I
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** Aparajitavarman comes last in the line of Pallava rulers (II PUC History, Ch 4.7, PDF p. 92); the dynasty ended with his defeat by the Cholas. He had nothing to do with the war against Pulakeshi II.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Nandivarman II was a later Pallava ruler of Kanchi, who was defeated by the Rashtrakutas and paid them tribute in elephants (II PUC History, Ch 4.8, PDF p. 96). He did not capture Vatapi.
**Option (c): Correct.** Pulakeshi II had defeated the Pallava king Mahendravarma. His son **Narasimhavarma I** took revenge by defeating Pulakeshi II and capturing **Vatapi**, which won him the titles **Mahamalla and Vatapikonda** (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 19, p. 25). He developed Mamallapura (Mahabalipuram) into a beautiful city (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 100).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Mahendravarma I is the father whose defeat by Pulakeshi II was avenged (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 19, p. 25). He is remembered as the author of the drama 'Matta Vilasa Prahasana' (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 19, p. 26).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Narasimhavarman I avenged his father Mahendravarman I by taking Vatapi from Pulakeshi II, and so became Mahamalla and Vatapikonda.

**Salient Features: The Pallavas at their height**
The Pallava dynasty, with its capital at Kanchi, reached its peak in the 7th century under Mahendravarman I and Narasimhavarman I (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 2, Ch 3).
- **'Mamalla':** the name means "wrestler" or "warrior". After capturing Badami he withdrew, keeping the Tungabhadra as an unwritten boundary between the two powers (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 2, Ch 3).
- **Sri Lanka:** Narasimhavarman I also sent a naval expedition to Sri Lanka to help a Sinhalese prince recover his throne (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 2, Ch 3).
- **Mahabalipuram:** monolithic chariot temples (rathas), each carved from a single stone, were built there during his rule; the relief called 'Gangavatarana' shows Bhagiratha performing penance to bring Ganga to the earth (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 100).
- **Religion at court:** DSERT records that the early Pallava kings were Buddhists and that Mahendravarma was a follower of Jainism (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 19, p. 26).

**Exam Fact:** The Shore Temple at Mamallapuram was built during the reign of Narasimhavarman II of the Pallava dynasty (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 2, Ch 3).

text:
Which of the three Sanskrit plays authored by King Harshavardhana is built on a Buddhist theme, depicting the self-sacrifice of the Naga prince Jimutavahana?
a) Ratnavali
b) Nagananda
c) Mudrarakshasa
d) Priyadarshika
sol:
**Correct Option: (b)**

**Justification:**
Harshavardhana himself wrote three plays in Sanskrit: **Priyadarshika, Ratnavali and Nagananda** (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 21).
**Option (a): Incorrect.** Ratnavali is one of Harsha's three plays, but it is a court romance, not the play on Jimutavahana's sacrifice.
**Option (b): Correct.** **Nagananda** is the play with the Buddhist theme: the Naga prince Jimutavahana offers his own body to save the nagas from Garuda.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** Mudrarakshasa is not Harsha's at all. It is the work of Vishakhadatta, of the Gupta period (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, p. 8).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Priyadarshika is also one of Harsha's three plays, but, like Ratnavali, it is a court romance.
Hence the correct answer is option (b).

**Result:** Of Harsha's three plays, Nagananda is the Buddhist one; Ratnavali and Priyadarshika are romances, and Mudrarakshasa is Vishakhadatta's.

**Salient Features: Harsha and his court**
DSERT describes Harshavardhana as a poet as well as a warrior (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 21).
- **The Vardhanas:** the kingdom of the Vardhanas, one of those that rose after the Gupta empire broke up, ruled from Thaneswar in the 6th century (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, p. 11).
- **Kanauj assembly:** the council at Kanauj went on for 23 days, and Hiuen Tsang explained the philosophy of Mahayana in it (II PUC History, Ch 4.7, PDF p. 83).
- **Prayag, 643 CE:** Harsha organised the Mahamoksha Parishat at Prayag, held once in five years; it lasted 75 days, and the image of the Buddha was taken in procession along with those of Shiva and Surya (II PUC History, Ch 4.7, PDF p. 83).
- **Hiuen Tsang's account:** much of what is known of daily life, dress and food in Harsha's time comes from it (Tamil Nadu History textbook, p. 130).

**Exam Fact:** Yasomatidevi, wife of Prabhakara Vardhana, immolated herself after her husband's death, an instance of sati in Harsha's family (Tamil Nadu History textbook, p. 130).

text:
Which term used in Gupta-period inscriptions denoted a levy of forced (unpaid) labour on the peasantry?
a) Bhaga
b) Udranga
c) Hiranya
d) Vishti
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** Bhaga was the king's customary share of the produce, normally one-sixth, paid by cultivators (Tamil Nadu History textbook, PDF p. 117). It is a tax in produce, not labour.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Udranga was an extra tax, explained either as a police tax for the upkeep of police stations or as a water tax (Tamil Nadu History textbook, PDF p. 117).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** Hiranya literally means a tax payable in gold coin, though in practice it was probably the king's share of certain crops paid in kind (Tamil Nadu History textbook, PDF p. 117). It is a tax, not labour.
**Option (d): Correct.** In the Gupta period the villagers of central and western India were subjected to forced labour called **vishti**, for serving the royal army and officials (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, Ch 20, PDF p. 152).
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Vishti is forced labour; bhaga, udranga and hiranya are all taxes.

**Salient Features: The Gupta revenue burden**
Gupta inscriptions name many dues, and the peasant's burden grew in this period.
- **Land against trade:** in the Gupta period land taxes increased in number and those on trade and commerce decreased; the king probably collected from one-fourth to one-sixth of the produce (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, Ch 20, PDF p. 152).
- **Feeding the army:** whenever the royal army passed through the countryside, the local people had to feed it, and peasants had to supply animals, foodgrains and furniture for royal officers on duty (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, Ch 20, PDF p. 152).
- **Other dues:** bhoga was a periodic supply of fruits, firewood and flowers to the king, and kara a periodic levy on villagers outside the annual land tax (Tamil Nadu History textbook, PDF p. 117).
- **Law:** R.S. Sharma notes that civil and criminal law were for the first time clearly defined and demarcated in this period (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, Ch 20, PDF p. 152).

**Exam Fact:** Halivakara was a plough tax paid by every cultivator who owned a plough (Tamil Nadu History textbook, PDF p. 117).

text:
Consider the following statements:

Statement I: Shams-ud-din Iltutmish, rather than Qutb-ud-din Aibak, is regarded by historians as the real founder of the Delhi Sultanate.
Statement II: Iltutmish shifted the capital of the Sultanate from Delhi to Lahore, to consolidate his power over the Punjab region.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
a) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I
b) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct, but Statement II is not the correct explanation of Statement I
c) Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
d) Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Statement I: Correct.** Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the Slave dynasty (II PUC History, Ch 5.1), but Satish Chandra holds that Iltutmish must be regarded as the real consolidator of the Turkish conquests in north India (Satish Chandra, *History of Medieval India*, PDF p. 93). Iltutmish defeated his rivals Yeldoz of Ghazni and Kabacha of Sindh, and the Khalif of Baghdad honoured him with a letter of authority (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, p. 14–15). This is why historians treat him as the real founder of the Sultanate.
**Statement II: Incorrect.** Iltutmish did not move the capital away from Delhi. Lahore and Multan were fought over by Iltutmish and his rivals Yalduz and Qubacha, and Iltutmish conquered both (Satish Chandra, *History of Medieval India*, PDF p. 101). He brought Lahore under Delhi; he did not make it his capital.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect, which is option (c). Options (a) and (b) accept the false Statement II, and option (d) rejects the correct Statement I.
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Iltutmish, not Aibak, consolidated the Sultanate and is called its real founder; he conquered Lahore but kept Delhi as his capital.

**Salient Features: Iltutmish**
Iltutmish turned a fragile conquest into a state.
- **Origin:** he belonged to the Ilbari tribe (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, p. 14).
- **Succession:** he was the son-in-law of Aibak and had to defeat Aibak's son before taking the throne, so the principle of a son succeeding his father was checked at the outset (Satish Chandra, *History of Medieval India*, PDF p. 93).
- **Iqtas:** he divided his kingdom into provinces (ikta) and appointed provincial officers (iktadars) to oversee their administration (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, p. 15).
- **Qutb Minar:** the tapering tower begun by Aibak was completed by Iltutmish (Satish Chandra, *History of Medieval India*, PDF p. 199).

**Exam Fact:** Finding none of his surviving sons worthy, Iltutmish nominated his daughter Raziya to the throne (Satish Chandra, *History of Medieval India*, PDF p. 94).

text:
In the context of the Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu, consider the following statements:
1. Andal, a woman Alvar, saw herself as the beloved of Vishnu, and her compositions continue to be sung today.
2. Compositions of the twelve Alvars were compiled into an anthology called the Nalayira Divyaprabandham, sometimes described as the 'Tamil Veda'.
3. The Tevaram anthology consists of poems by the Nayanar saints Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, classified on the basis of their music.
4. An inscription of around 945 CE records that the Chola ruler Parantaka I consecrated metal images of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in a Shiva temple.
Which of the above statements are correct?
a) 1, 2 and 3 only
b) 1 and 2 only
c) 1, 2, 3 and 4
d) 2, 3 and 4 only
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** The compositions of Andal, a woman Alvar, were widely sung and continue to be sung to date; Andal saw herself as the beloved of Vishnu (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 144).
**Statement 2: Correct.** By the tenth century the compositions of the 12 Alvars were compiled in the **Nalayira Divyaprabandham** ("Four Thousand Sacred Compositions"), which was frequently described as the **Tamil Veda** (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 144).
**Statement 3: Correct.** The poems of **Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar** form the Tevaram, a collection compiled and classified in the tenth century on the basis of the music of the songs (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 144).
**Statement 4: Correct.** Inscriptional evidence from around 945 suggests that the Chola ruler **Parantaka I** consecrated metal images of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in a Shiva temple; these were carried in processions during the saints' festivals (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 146).
All four statements are correct, which is option (c). Options (a), (b) and (d) each leave out at least one correct statement.
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Andal's songs, the Nalayira Divyaprabandham, the Tevaram and Parantaka I's metal images of the three Nayanars are all correctly described.

**Salient Features: The Alvars and Nayanars**
The Alvars were devotees of Vishnu and the Nayanars devotees of Shiva.
- **Karaikkal Ammaiyar:** a woman devotee of Shiva, she adopted the path of extreme asceticism (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 144).
- **Shrines:** during their travels the Alvars and Nayanars identified certain shrines as abodes of their deities, and large temples were often built at these places later (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 145).
- **Caste:** some historians suggest the two traditions began a movement of protest against the caste system, since the bhaktas came from backgrounds ranging from Brahmanas to artisans and cultivators (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 145).
- **Chola patronage:** the Chola kings introduced the singing of Tamil Shaiva hymns in temples under royal patronage (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 146).

**Exam Fact:** Both the Nayanars and the Alvars were revered by the Vellala peasants (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 6, p. 146).

text:
With reference to the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, consider the following statements:
1. It was erected by Heliodorus, an ambassador sent by the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to the court of the Sunga ruler Bhagabhadra.
2. The pillar is crowned by a figure of Garuda and was dedicated to the worship of Vasudeva (Vishnu).
3. In the inscription, Heliodorus describes himself as a follower of the Buddha.
4. The pillar is located near Vidisha in present-day Madhya Pradesh.
Which of the above statements are correct?
a) 1, 2 and 4 only
b) 1, 3 and 4 only
c) 1 and 2 only
d) 2, 3 and 4 only
sol:
**Correct Option: (a)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** The Indo-Greek king **Antialcidas** is known chiefly because his emissary, **Heliodorus**, was sent to the court of King **Bhagabhadra** (Tamil Nadu History textbook, p. 93).
**Statement 2: Correct.** Heliodorus erected a pillar, or garuda-dhvaja, whose capital is adorned with a figure of **Garuda**, in honour of **Vasudeva** (Krishna); he had evidently become a follower of Vishnu (Tamil Nadu History textbook, p. 93).
**Statement 3: Incorrect.** In his inscription Heliodorus praises Vasudeva as the "god of gods" (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, p. 135). He was a devotee of Vasudeva, not a follower of the Buddha. The Indo-Greek ruler who turned to Buddhism was Menander (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, PDF p. 120).
**Statement 4: Correct.** The Heliodorus pillar stands near **Vidisha**, Madhya Pradesh (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, p. 134).
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, which is option (a). Options (b) and (d) include the false 3; option (c) omits the true 4.
Hence the correct answer is option (a).

**Result:** Heliodorus, envoy of Antialcidas to Bhagabhadra, set up a Garuda pillar for Vasudeva near Vidisha; he was a Vaishnava, not a Buddhist.

**Salient Features: Indo-Greeks and Indian religion**
NCERT uses the Heliodorus pillar as its example of cultural exchange between the Indo-Greeks and India.
- **Three precepts:** the inscription says three immortal precepts, self-restraint, charity and consciousness, lead to heaven when practised (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, p. 135).
- **Coins:** Indo-Greek coins were made of gold, silver, copper and nickel; most show a king on one side and Greek deities on the other, but some depict Indian deities such as Vasudeva-Krishna and Lakshmi (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, p. 135).
- **Assimilation:** Manu described the Sakas and the Parthians as kshatriyas who had fallen from their duties (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, PDF p. 120).
- **End of Indo-Greek rule:** it ended with the invasions of the Indo-Scythians or Shakas (NCERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, p. 135).

**Exam Fact:** Menander's questions to the Buddhist teacher Nagasena, and Nagasena's answers, are recorded in the Milinda Panho, "The Questions of Milinda" (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, PDF p. 116).

text:
Match the pioneers of early Kannada prose/novel writing in List I with the fact associated with each in List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Lakshman Gadagkar | I. Wrote 'Suryakantha' (1892), the first original social novel in Kannada |
| B. Gulvadi Venkata Rao | II. Wrote 'Indira Bayi' (1899), an early landmark Kannada novel |
| C. Galaganatha (Venkata Thirko Kulkarni) | III. Adapted Marathi novelist Hari Narayan Apte's works into Kannada |
| D. Kerur Vasudevacharya | IV. Edited the Dharwad literary journal 'Shubhodaya' (1918) |

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
a) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
b) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
c) A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
d) A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
sol:
**Correct Option: (a)**

**Justification:**
The correct matching is **A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV**.
- **A-I:** the first original social novel in Kannada, Suryakantha, was published in 1892 by Lakshman Gadagkar (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 282; Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 136).
- **B-II:** it was followed by Gulvadi Venkatarao's Indirabayi (1899) (Kamath, p. 282).
- **C-III:** novels translated from Marathi by Galaganatha helped popularise the new literature (Kamath, p. 282); the historical novels of Hari Narayan Apte were translated into Kannada by Galaganatha (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 964).
- **D-IV:** this leaves the Dharwad journal Shubhodaya with Kerur Vasudevacharya, who is also named among the early Kannada short-story writers (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 139).

**Option (a): Correct.** It gives A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** A-I and B-II are right, but it swaps C and D, giving the journal to Galaganatha and the Apte adaptations to Kerur Vasudevacharya.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** All four pairs are wrong.
**Option (d): Incorrect.** It swaps the two novels, giving Suryakantha to Gulvadi Venkata Rao and Indirabayi to Gadagkar.
Hence the correct answer is option (a).

**Result:** Suryakantha (1892) is Gadagkar's, Indirabayi (1899) Gulvadi Venkata Rao's; Galaganatha adapted Apte's Marathi novels, and Shubhodaya goes with Kerur Vasudevacharya.

**Salient Features: Early modern Kannada prose and stage**
The Kannada novel grew out of translation before original works appeared.
- **Translations first:** social novels had already been translated from English, Marathi and Bengali before Suryakantha appeared (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 136).
- **The stage:** the Handbook names Iggappa Heggadeya Prahasana (1887) by Venkatarama Shastry as the first original Kannada social play, and new drama troupes came up at Gadag (1874) and Halasangi, with another at Mysuru (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 136).
- **A reformist novel:** Gulvadi Venkatrao's Indirabai condemned the ban on sea travel then observed by orthodox castes (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. 504).
- **The short story:** Masti Venkatesha Iyengar, Panje Mangesha Rao, M.N. Kamath and Kerur Vasudevacharya were among the early short-story writers (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 139).

**Exam Fact:** Bengali novels were brought into Kannada by B. Venkatachar (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 282).

text:
Match List I (Jain Tirthankara) with List II (associated symbol):

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Chandraprabha | I. Serpent (snake) |
| B. Shantinatha | II. Deer |
| C. Neminatha | III. Moon (crescent) |
| D. Parshvanatha | IV. Conch shell |

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
a) A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
b) A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I
c) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
d) A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
The correct matching is **A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I**.
- **A-III:** the symbol (lanchhana) of Chandraprabha is the moon, as his name, "moon-light", suggests.
- **B-II:** the symbol of Shantinatha is the deer.
- **C-IV:** the symbol of Neminatha is the conch shell.
- **D-I:** the symbol of Parshvanatha is the serpent; his images show him beneath a canopy of snake hoods.

**Option (a): Incorrect.** A-III and D-I are right, but it gives the conch to Shantinatha and the deer to Neminatha.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** It exchanges the moon and the conch between Chandraprabha and Neminatha.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** It exchanges the serpent and the moon between Chandraprabha and Parshvanatha.
**Option (d): Correct.** It gives A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Moon for Chandraprabha, deer for Shantinatha, conch for Neminatha, serpent for Parshvanatha.

**Salient Features: Jain worship in Karnataka**
The Karnataka Gazetteer describes how Jain worship was organised in the state (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. 425).
- **In the bastis:** tirthankaras such as Adinatha, Parshwanatha and Neminatha are worshipped, along with Yakshas and Yakshis.
- **Yakshis:** Padmavati and Jwalamalini are very popular in Karnataka.
- **The West Coast:** in Vijayanagara times Jaina princes of Gersoppa, Karkal and Mudabidre erected Jaina monuments at Bhatkal, Karkal and Mudabidre.
- **Dharmasthala:** one more Gomata monolith was erected at Dharmasthala in 1982.

**Exam Fact:** Humcha is a centre of the worship of the Yakshi Padmavati (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. 425).

text:
The core of the Great Stupa at Sanchi is believed to have originally been built, in brick, during the reign of which ruler, and was later enlarged with a stone casing and railings?
a) Kanishka
b) Chandragupta Maurya
c) Harshavardhana
d) Ashoka
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** Kanishka was a Kushan ruler (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 16, p. 4) of a much later period than the first stupa at Sanchi.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Chandragupta Maurya, Ashoka's grandfather, is remembered for his palace at Pataliputra (II PUC History, Ch 4.3, PDF p. 59). The building of stupas over the Buddha's relics is credited to Ashoka, not to him.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** Harshavardhana ruled in the seventh century; the Vardhanas themselves rose only in the 6th century (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, p. 11). By then the Sanchi stupa had stood for centuries.
**Option (d): Correct.** According to the Buddhist text Ashokavadana, **Ashoka** distributed portions of the Buddha's relics to every important town and ordered the construction of stupas over them; by the second century BCE stupas at Bharhut, Sanchi and Sarnath had been built (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 96). The original brick stupa at Sanchi belongs to his reign.
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Sanchi's first brick stupa goes back to Ashoka, who, by Buddhist tradition, had stupas built over the Buddha's relics.

**Salient Features: The Sanchi stupa**
NCERT describes Sanchi as among the best preserved monuments of early India (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 82).
- **Railings and gateways:** the early stupas at Sanchi and Bharhut were plain except for stone railings, which resembled a bamboo or wooden fence, and richly carved gateways at the four cardinal points (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 97).
- **Donors:** inscriptions on the railings and pillars record donations by kings such as the Satavahanas, by guilds, by men and women, and by monks and nuns (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 96).
- **Preservation:** the rulers of Bhopal, Shahjehan Begum and her successor Sultan Jehan Begum, provided money for the preservation of the site (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 83).
- **A Jataka in stone:** a gateway scene once read as a rural view is identified by art historians as the Vessantara Jataka (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 99).

**Exam Fact:** A guild of ivory workers financed part of one of the gateways at Sanchi (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 96).

text:
Which one of the following statements about the royal houses of Karnataka is NOT correct?
a) The Nayakas of Chitradurga came originally from Medhakeri near Tirupati and began as palegars under Vijayanagara.
b) The Wodeyar dynasty began with the brothers Yaduraya and Krishnaraya, who came to Mysore from Dwaraka in Gujarat.
c) Tailapa II, the founder of the dynasty of the Chalukyas of Kalyana, built the city of Kalyana and made it his capital.
d) The Nayakas of Keladi were also called the Nayakas of Ikkeri.
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** The statement is accurate, so it is not the answer. The Nayakas of Chitradurga were originally from Medhakeri near Tirupati in Andhra and settled at Chitradurga. They started their career as palegars during the Vijayanagara period and belonged to the Beda community (II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 155).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** The statement is accurate. Yaduraya and his brother Krishnaraya came to Mysore from Dwaraka in Gujarat. Yaduraya killed the dalvoy Maranayaka, and the Maharani gave her daughter to him in marriage; thus the Wodeyar dynasty began (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 46).
**Option (c): Correct.** The statement is false, so it is the answer. Tailapa II did establish the kingdom of the Chalukyas of Kalyana, but it was **Someshwara I** who built the new city of **Kalyana** and made it his capital (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 35).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** The statement is accurate. The Nayakas of Keladi were also called the Nayakas of Ikkeri (II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 154).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Tailapa II founded the Kalyana Chalukya kingdom, but the city of Kalyana was built by Someshwara I; the Chitradurga, Wodeyar and Keladi statements are accurate.

**Salient Features: Royal houses of Karnataka**
After the Vijayanagara empire disintegrated, various Nayakas, palegars and small rulers became independent (II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 154).
- **Tailapa II:** he had been a tributary king of the Rashtrakutas. He defeated the Rashtrakuta king Karka II, established the kingdom of the Kalyana Chalukyas and ruled for about 24 years (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 35).
- **Someshwara I in war:** though he had to wage many wars, he kept his kingdom from shrinking (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 35).
- **Keladi:** the Nayakas of Keladi came to power in the 16th century and ruled for about 250 years over parts of Karnataka, Kerala and Goa. Linganna Kavi wrote the historical work "Keladi Nrupavijayam" (II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF pp. 154–155).
- **Chitradurga:** Hyder Ali besieged the Chitradurga fort, which had seven concentric walls. Madakari Nayaka was defeated in a later siege, imprisoned and killed, and with him the dynasty of the Nayakas of Chitradurga came to an end (DSERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 7, PDF p. 106).
- **Wodeyars:** the dynasty was ruled by 25 Wodeyars, from Yaduraya to Jayachamaraja Wodeyar (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 46).

**Exam Fact:** During Hyder Ali's siege of Chitradurga, Onake Obavva, the wife of a watchman of the fort, killed many enemy soldiers with a pestle (onake); "Obavva's Kindi" lies to the west of the fort (DSERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 7, PDF p. 106; II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 155).

text:
In the context of cultural life at the Mughal court, the following statements are made:
1. Faizi translated the mathematical work "Leelavati" into Persian.
2. Daswant and Basawan were famous painters at the court of Jahangir.
3. The musicians of Akbar's court were divided into seven groups, each group giving a concert on a particular day.
4. Ustad Mansoor was a painter at the court of Jahangir.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
a) 1, 2, 3 and 4
b) 1 and 3 only
c) 2, 3 and 4 only
d) 1, 3 and 4 only
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** **Faizi** translated the mathematical work **Leelavati** into Persian (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 12).
**Statement 2: Incorrect.** Daswant and Basawan were famous painters at the court of **Akbar**, not Jahangir (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 13).
**Statement 3: Correct.** The musicians of Akbar's court were divided into seven groups, and each group gave a concert on a particular day (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 15, PDF p. 76).
**Statement 4: Correct.** **Ustad Mansoor** was a painter at Jahangir's court (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 13).
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct, which is option (d). Options (a) and (c) include the false 2, and option (b) omits the true 4.
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Faizi translated Leelavati, Akbar's musicians played in seven groups and Mansoor painted for Jahangir; Daswant and Basawan were Akbar's painters.

**Salient Features: Painting and learning at the Mughal court**
The Mughal court supported translation, painting and music.
- **Beginnings of Mughal painting:** the art of painting evolved in Humayun's time with the help of Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad of Persia (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 13).
- **Akbar's artists:** of the 17 artists at Akbar's court, 13 were Hindus; besides Daswant and Basawan, Lala and Mukund are named (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 13).
- **Jahangir's artists:** Ustad Mansoor and Abul Hasan (Abdul Hassan) worked at his court (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 13).
- **Translations into Persian:** besides Faizi's Leelavati, Raja Todar Mal translated the Bhagavata Purana into Persian (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 12).

**Exam Fact:** Tansen is named as the most remarkable of the musicians at Akbar's court (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 15, PDF p. 76).

text:
Sher Shah, the founder of the Sur dynasty, was originally named
a) Ibrahim Khan
b) Bahar Khan
c) Hasan Khan
d) Farid Khan
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** Ibrahim Sur was Sher Shah's grandfather, who came to India from Afghanistan (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 38). It was not Sher Shah's own name.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Bahar Khan Lohani, the ruler of South Bihar, was the master in whose service Farid earned the name Sher Khan (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 6).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** Hasan Khan (Hasan Sur) was Sher Shah's father, who held the iqta of Sahsaram (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF pp. 38–39).
**Option (d): Correct.** Sher Shah belonged to the Sur clan of Afghanistan; his original name was Farid Khan, and he founded the Sur dynasty (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 6).
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Farid Khan became Sher Khan and then Sher Shah; Hasan was his father, Ibrahim his grandfather and Bahar Khan Lohani his patron.

**Salient Features: Sher Shah Sur**
Sher Shah's kingdom comprised the whole of North India except Assam, Gujarat and Kashmir (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 6).
- **Early training:** his father gave him charge of his two parganas (1515–16), which gave the young Farid first-hand experience of administration at the pargana and village levels (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 39).
- **Victory over Humayun:** he defeated Humayun at Chausa (March 1539) and Kanauj (May 1540) (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 232). Humayun came back to power only after Sher Shah's death (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 6).
- **Highways:** he built and improved four main highways. The one from Sonargaon to the banks of the Indus through Agra, Delhi and Lahore was called the Sadak-e-Azam, and shade-giving trees and 1,700 sarais were provided along them (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 6).
- **Forts:** he constructed new forts at Rohtas, Delhi, Kanauj and Patna (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 7).

**Exam Fact:** For his impartial justice, Sher Shah earned the title "Sultan of fair justice" (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 7).

text:
Which Later Vedic sacrifice involved a ritual chariot race in which the king's chariot was made to win against his kinsmen, marking his political supremacy?
a) Rajasuya
b) Vajapeya
c) Ashvamedha
d) Upanayana
sol:
**Correct Option: (b)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** The rajasuya sacrifice was supposed to confer supreme power on the king (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56). It is a royal consecration, not a chariot race.
**Option (b): Correct.** The king performed the **vajapeya**, or the chariot race, in which the royal chariot was made to win the race against his kinsmen (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** The ashvamedha meant unquestioned control over the area in which the royal horse ran uninterrupted (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56); a battle followed if the horse was challenged (Tamil Nadu History textbook, PDF p. 39).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Upanayana is investiture with the sacred thread, to which the three higher varnas were entitled (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56). It is a rite of the individual, not a royal sacrifice.
Hence the correct answer is option (b).

**Result:** Vajapeya was the royal chariot race; rajasuya conferred supreme power, ashvamedha claimed territory through the horse, and upanayana is the sacred-thread rite.

**Salient Features: Later Vedic kingship**
The king's influence was strengthened by rituals in the later Vedic period (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56).
- **Priests:** elaborate sacrifices such as the rajasuya and ashvamedha were performed by chiefs and kings who depended on Brahmana priests to conduct them (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 84).
- **Taxes:** collection of taxes and tributes seems to have become common, and they were probably deposited with an officer called the sangrihitri (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56).
- **The king's helpers:** the king was assisted by the priest, the commander, the chief queen and a few other high functionaries (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56).
- **The chariot-maker:** certain artisans such as the rathakara, or chariot-maker, enjoyed high status and were entitled to the sacred thread ceremony (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 57).

**Exam Fact:** In the later Vedic period taxes and tributes were probably deposited with an officer called the sangrihitri (R.S. Sharma, *Ancient India*, p. 56).

text:
Consider the following statements about Vijayanagara-period temple architecture at Hampi.
1. Temples of this period became larger in scale, with pillared halls and separate 'Kalyana Mantapas' built for the ceremonial wedding of deities.
2. The Vijaya Vittala temple at Hampi is famous for its musical (saptaswara) pillars and its stone chariot.
3. The 'Utsava Mantapa' found in these temple complexes was meant exclusively for the coronation of kings.
4. Vijayanagara temple complexes were typically enclosed within a cloistered corridor (prakara), along with subsidiary shrines.
How many of the above statements are correct?
a) Only one
b) Only two
c) Only three
d) 1, 2, 3 and 4
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** A distinctive feature of Vijayanagara architecture was the building of huge halls and marriage halls (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, p. 39). The kalyana mandapa was meant to celebrate divine weddings (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 7, p. 186).
**Statement 2: Correct.** The Vijaya Vitthala temple at Hampi is known for its saptaswara musical pillars, huge Kalyana Mantapas and the Stone Chariot (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, p. 40).
**Statement 3: Incorrect.** The Utsava Mantapa is one of the temple's own buildings, standing with the Kalyana Mantapa inside the Vitthala complex (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 1053). As its name (utsava, festival) shows, it served the deity's festivals; it was not meant exclusively for crowning kings.
**Statement 4: Correct.** The Vitthala temple is a fully developed temple with the Kalyana and Utsava Mantapas within a cloistered enclosure pierced by three entrance gopurams (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 1053), and long pillared corridors often ran around the shrines within such complexes (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 7, p. 186).
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, so the count is three, which is option (c).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Kalyana mandapas, the Vitthala temple's pillars and chariot, and cloistered enclosures are right; the Utsava Mantapa was a festival hall, not a coronation hall.

**Salient Features: Vijayanagara temple building**
The Handbook calls the Vitthala temple the culmination of Vijayanagara temple architecture (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 1053).
- **Raya gopurams:** royal gateways of immense scale were a mark of imperial authority and signalled the presence of the temple from a great distance (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 7, p. 185).
- **Vitthala:** the principal deity is a form of Vishnu generally worshipped in Maharashtra, an example of how the rulers drew on different traditions (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 7, p. 188).
- **Chariot streets:** they ran straight from the temple gopuram, were paved with stone slabs and were lined with pillared pavilions in which merchants set up shops (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 7, p. 188).
- **Shringeri:** DSERT names the Vidyashankara temple at Shringeri as the most important temple built at the beginning of Vijayanagara rule (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, p. 39).

**Exam Fact:** The Vitthala complex has a large pushkarani (stepped tank) with a Vasantotsava mantapa, a ceremonial pavilion, at its centre (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 1053).

text:
Arrange the following religious teachers in the chronological order of their birth:
1. Madhvacharya
2. Guru Nanak
3. Shankaracharya
4. Ramanujacharya

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
a) 4-3-1-2
b) 3-4-1-2
c) 3-1-4-2
d) 3-4-2-1
sol:
**Correct Option: (b)**

**Justification:**
**Correct sequence:** 3 **Shankaracharya**, born at Kaladi in Kerala in **788 CE** (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 165); 4 **Ramanujacharya**, born in **1017 CE** at Sri Perambadur near Chennai (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 166); 1 **Madhvacharya**, born at Pajaka near Udupi in **1238 CE** (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 167); 2 **Guru Nanak**, born in **1469 CE** (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 172). That gives **3-4-1-2**.
**Option (a): Incorrect.** 4-3-1-2 puts Ramanujacharya (1017) before Shankaracharya (788).
**Option (b): Correct.** 3-4-1-2 matches 788, 1017, 1238 and 1469.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** 3-1-4-2 puts Madhvacharya (1238) before Ramanujacharya (1017).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** 3-4-2-1 puts Guru Nanak (1469) before Madhvacharya (1238).
Hence the correct answer is option (b).

**Result:** Shankaracharya (788), Ramanujacharya (1017), Madhvacharya (1238), Guru Nanak (1469).

**Salient Features: Three acharyas and three philosophies**
Each of the three acharyas founded a distinct school of Vedanta.
- **Shankaracharya, Advaita:** Advaita means monism or non-duality. He bore the titles "Sarvajna" and "Jagadguru" (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF pp. 165–166).
- **Ramanujacharya, Vishishtadvaita:** he was the propounder of Vishishtadvaita philosophy (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 166).
- **Madhvacharya, Dvaita:** he taught that the individual soul and God are two different entities, and he recognised five fundamental differences between soul, matter and God (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 168).
- **Guru Nanak:** he was the founder of Sikhism (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 172).

**Exam Fact:** Madhvacharya was born at Pajaka near Udupi in 1238 CE (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 167).

text:
Match the Karnataka dynasty/royal house in List I with its royal emblem in List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Hoysalas | I. Golden eagle (Garuda) |
| B. Chalukyas of Badami | II. Gandaberunda (two-headed eagle) |
| C. Rashtrakutas of Malkhed | III. Varaha (divine boar) |
| D. Wodeyars of Mysore | IV. Sala killing a tiger |

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
a) A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II
b) A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV
c) A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
d) A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
The correct matching is **A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II**.
- **A-IV:** the Hoysala emblem depicts Sala slaying a tiger (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 109).
- **B-III:** Varaha was the royal emblem of the Badami Chalukyas (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 96).
- **C-I:** Garuda was the royal emblem of the Rashtrakutas (II PUC History, Ch 4.8, PDF p. 95).
- **D-II:** the royal emblem of the Wodeyars of Mysore was the Ganda-Bherunda (DSERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 72).

**Option (a): Incorrect.** A-IV and D-II are right, but it exchanges the Varaha and the Garuda between the Chalukyas and the Rashtrakutas.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** B-III and C-I are right, but it exchanges the Sala-and-tiger and the Ganda-Bherunda between the Hoysalas and the Wodeyars.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** A-IV and B-III are right, but it exchanges the Garuda and the Ganda-Bherunda between the Rashtrakutas and the Wodeyars.
**Option (d): Correct.** It gives A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Hoysalas: Sala killing a tiger; Badami Chalukyas: Varaha; Rashtrakutas: Garuda; Wodeyars: Ganda-Bherunda.

**Salient Features: Royal emblems of Karnataka**
Each ruling house of Karnataka had its own crest.
- **Kadambas and Gangas:** the emblem of the Kadambas was a lion, and that of the Gangas an elephant, the madhagaja (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 92, 95).
- **The Sala story:** a Jaina muni ordered the youth Sala, "Poy Sala" ("Strike, O Sala"), when a tiger appeared; Sala killed it, and the family came to be called Poysala (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 129).
- **A possible meaning:** Kamath suggests the story may stand for the early Hoysala successes against the Cholas, whose royal emblem was the tiger (Kamath, p. 130).
- **Garuda and faith:** the Rashtrakutas were Vaishnavas, as their royal emblem Garuda suggests (Kamath, p. 100).

**Exam Fact:** The Sala story appears for the first time in the Beluru record of Vishnuvardhana dated 1117 (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 129).

text:
Consider the following statements regarding cultural developments under the Chalukyas of Kalyana:
1. Bilhana, a poet from Kashmir, composed Vikramankadeva Charita with Vikramaditya VI as its hero.
2. Vijnaneshwara wrote Mitakshara, a commentary on Yajnavalkya Smriti, in the court of Someshwara III.
3. Someshwara III compiled the Sanskrit encyclopaedia Manasollasa, also called Abhilashitartha Chintamani.
4. The Mahadeva temple at Itagi, praised in an inscription as 'Devalaya Chakravarti', was built by Mahadeva, a commander of Vikramaditya VI.
How many of the above statements are correct?
a) Only one
b) Only two
c) Only three
d) 1, 2, 3 and 4
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** Bilhana, a poet from Kashmir, came to Kalyana in search of a patron (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. vii), and wrote the Vikramankadeva-charita, a biography of Vikramaditya VI (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 104).
**Statement 2: Incorrect.** Vijnaneshwara, author of the Mitakshara, was an outstanding scholar in the court of **Vikramaditya VI** (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 104), who ruled 1076–1127 (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. vii). Someshwara III was Vikramaditya VI's son and successor.
**Statement 3: Correct.** Someshwara III wrote the Manasollasa in Sanskrit (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 104), a work also called the Abhilashitartha Chintamani (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. 249).
**Statement 4: Correct.** Mahadeva, one of Vikramaditya VI's commanders, built the Mahadeva temple at Itagi in Koppal district, which an inscription eulogises as "Devalaya Chakravarthy", the emperor among temples (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 124; Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 112).
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct, so the count is three, which is option (c).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Bilhana and Vijnaneshwara both served Vikramaditya VI; his son Someshwara III wrote the Manasollasa, and his commander Mahadeva built the Itagi temple.

**Salient Features: Kalyana under Vikramaditya VI and his son**
DSERT calls Vikramaditya VI the greatest emperor of the dynasty (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 104).
- **Titles:** Vikramaditya VI bore the titles Permadideva and Tribhuvanamalla (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 112).
- **Praise from his scholars:** Bilhana describes his rule as Ramarajya, and Vijnaneshvara says a king like Vikramarka is neither seen nor heard of (Kamath, p. 112).
- **Itagi praised:** Dr. Cousens called the Itagi temple "the finest in Kannada country after Halebidu" (Kamath, p. 125).
- **Manasollasa as a record:** it speaks of eight varieties of rice and classifies wells by the number of their outlets (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. 581, 668).

**Exam Fact:** Jagadekamalla II of the Kalyana Chalukyas wrote the Sangeeta Chudamani, a work on music and dance (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, p. 35).
